query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of equimolar HEA nanoparticles over a wide temperature range (473–1923 K) is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and kinetic hindrance from lattice distortion. In nanoparticles with pronounced lattice distortion (due to larger atomic size mismatches), sluggish atomic diffusion kinetically stabilizes the homogeneous solid solution even under severe catalytic (reducing) and thermoelectric (mildly oxidizing) conditions. In contrast, HEAs with minimal lattice distortion overcome kinetic barriers at high temperatures, leading to surface segregation or phase decomposition.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar HEA nanoparticles crystallized as a single-phase solid solution with uniform elemental distribution (e.g., a CrMnFeCoNi-type alloy)
generation.intervention: Synthesize two sets of equimolar HEA nanoparticles: one set with enhanced lattice distortion (by intentionally including metals with greater atomic radii variation) and a comparative set with lower lattice distortion (using metals with more similar atomic sizes). Subject both sets to repeated thermal cycling from 473 K up to 1923 K under two atmospheres: a reducing (catalytic) environment and a mildly oxidizing (thermoelectric) environment.
generation.conditions: Controlled temperature cycling (473–1923 K) with defined ramp rates and dwell times, under strictly regulated atmospheres (inert/reducing versus mildly oxidizing) that mimic catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of lattice distortion which sets the kinetic barrier (i.e., atomic diffusion rate) counterbalancing the thermodynamic drive (mixing enthalpy versus –TΔSmix) for phase separation or elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy thermodynamically favors a single-phase solid solution. However, at elevated temperatures, increased atomic vibrations tend to overcome mixing barriers. If significant lattice distortion is present, the resulting high diffusion barriers induce sluggish atomic migration, preserving homogeneous elemental distribution. In environments that promote oxidation (thermoelectric conditions), insufficient kinetic hindrance could allow differential surface diffusion and segregation, destabilizing the phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with higher lattice distortion will maintain uniform solid solution structures and catalytic performance across the 473–1923 K range in both catalytic and thermoelectric atmospheres. In contrast, nanoparticles with lower lattice distortion will show measurable elemental segregation, phase decomposition, and corresponding changes in catalytic activity—especially under the oxidizing (thermoelectric) conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles show a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with nearly equimolar elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for equimolar HEAs where the dominant differences arise solely from the degree of lattice distortion. Deviations may occur if particle size, support interactions, or extreme non-controlled atmospheres dominate the kinetic processes. Also, behavior beyond 1923 K or under conditions with extreme redox potentials might differ.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on evidence from PMC7069714 (which showed that multi-element mixing induces lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion) and PMC11247481 (which linked configurational entropy with active site stability in HEAs). The new element is the controlled comparison of HEAs with different degrees of lattice distortion under both catalytic and thermoelectric conditions—a factor not directly addressed in earlier studies. Uncertainties remain regarding the quantitative impact of vibrational and surface energy contributions at the upper end of the temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nanoparticle ensembles of the same equimolar composition but differing in lattice distortion (achieved by selecting metals with either large or similar atomic radii). Subject both ensembles to identical thermal cycling (473–1923 K) while alternating between a reducing atmosphere (mimicking catalytic operation) and a mildly oxidizing atmosphere (mimicking thermoelectric operation). Monitor the structural evolution in situ using techniques such as high-resolution TEM, atom probe tomography, and XRD, and correlate these with catalytic performance measurements (e.g., activity tests for a model reaction).
measurements: High-resolution TEM imaging for nanoparticle morphology and phase identification
Atom probe tomography or EDS mapping for elemental distribution
XRD for phase changes and detection of any segregation or new phase formation
In situ diffusion measurements (or tracer experiments) to assess atomic mobility
Catalytic performance tests to track changes in activity associated with structural degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion fail to show improved structural and chemical stability (e.g., they display similar or greater levels of surface segregation and phase decomposition compared to the low-distortion ensemble), or if both sets exhibit indistinguishable stability profiles and catalytic performance across the entire temperature range and atmospheres, then the hypothesis—that lattice distortion imparts kinetic stabilization against high-temperature de-mixing—is falsified.

As depicted in Figure 1, our framework encompasses three main components: phase stability evaluation using empirical thermodynamic rules, surface modeling of HEA nanoparticles through large-scale Monte Carlo simulations driven by deep learning interatomic potentials, and activity prediction via the integration of a pretrained theory-infused neural network (TinNet) that accurately predicts the surface reactivity of metal sites with a descriptor-based electrokinetic model. This framework successfully captures the enhanced ORR activity of the PdCuPtNiCo HEA nanoparticle system compared to pure Pt as observed in our experiment and elucidates the reactivity origin of HEA surface sites within the framework of the d-band theory. The framework not only facilitates accurate modeling of HEA catalysis but also advances our fundamental understanding of high-entropy materials’ surface reactivity, potentially accelerating the design and synthesis of monodisperse HEA nanoparticle catalysts for sustainable chemical and energy transformations.

Resistive heating up to 723 K in a DAC was performed on the high-pressure recovered hcp HEA sample at the beamline 12.2.2 of the Advanced Light Source, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The hcp-structured CoCrFeMnNi HEA for the heating experiment was synthesized by compressing the original fcc-structured CoCrFeMnNi HEA to 35 GPa and then decompressing it to ambient pressure in a DAC at room temperature. The wavelength of the X-ray was ∼0.4959 Å, and the beam size was 20 × 20 μm2. 2D XRD images were collected using a Mar345 image plate. To achieve higher temperatures and study the stability the hcp phase at higher pressures, a complementary online laser heating system coupled with DACs at the beamline 13-ID-D, APS, ANL was employed to perform double-sided laser heating on the hcp phased sample. The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ).
